Say what the stop is before setting off. Check the current opening hours and the practical access details that matter to you. Bring the needed mobility and communication supports. Decide how to turn back before leaving. On a wet or cold day, looking out together and planning a future walk may be plenty. title: A Little Way Down the Trail with Great-Aunt Susan
summary: A short walk at Minute Man with James and Great-Aunt Susan: Revolutionary history, sensory discoveries, and the pleasure of going at his pace.
search: Minute Man National Historical Park · From the family albumA Little Way Down the Trail with Great-Aunt SusanA short walk at Minute Man National Historical Park, a very good tree, and the pleasure of having someone join you right where you are.October 20, 2026 · A family journal James and Great-Aunt Susan, with plenty to show for a short walk. When James’s great-aunt Susan came to visit, we took her for a walk at Minute Man National Historical Park, near our home. We didn’t go very far that day. We did, however, give one particular tree a considerable amount of attention. It had deeply ridged bark and roots rising through the grass. Behind it, a stone wall ran between the trees. There were leaves underfoot, bare branches overhead, and quite enough to occupy us without getting much farther down the path. James had a small piece of wood. Susan had a twig. In the photographs, they’re both beside the trunk, exploring. In one, James has his hand against the bark. In another, he’s grinning while Susan holds her twig toward the tree. I love seeing them together like this. Susan knows how to join him One of the things I appreciate most about Susan is the way she meets James where he is. She notices what interests him and finds something to share with him there. On this walk, that meant the sensory pleasures of nature: texture, things to look at closely, something interesting happening at the base of a tree. Susan could see the possibilities in what was already around them. She was willing to stay and explore. As his mother, I’m grateful for that kind of attention. I want James to have people in his life who get to know his interests, enjoy his company, and make room for his way of participating. Susan does that with such warmth. One tree, two sticks, and time together. And there is plenty of humor in these pictures. In one of the photographs on the path, they’re both laughing. James has his bag of Goldfish. Susan is holding the tablet in its blue case. A few frames later, her arm is around his shoulders and they’re smiling at the camera. The Goldfish have made it into the family portrait, too. Fair enough. They came on the walk. A little Minute Man history, with Susan Susan was enamored with the history of the area, and Minute Man gives you plenty to think about as you walk. The park preserves historic places in Lexington, Lincoln, and Concord associated with April 19, 1775, when the opening battles of the American Revolution unfolded here. Read the National Park Service’s history of that day. Today, the park’s five-mile Battle Road Trail connects historic sites between Concord and Lexington. Much of it follows surviving portions of the historic Battle Road; other stretches leave the old road and pass through fields, wetlands, and woods. Explore the Battle Road Trail. I loved sharing this part of home with Susan. When a place is familiar, someone else’s enthusiasm gives you a reason to look again. The stone walls, the paths, the stories attached to the landscape: she was interested in all of it. And she brought that same curiosity to her time with James. There she was beside the tree, with a twig of her own, joining him. There was room for the history, the sensory discoveries, and the pleasure of being together. We could take our time with all three. A pause on the path with Susan. And the Goldfish. How far we went Looking back through the photographs, I’m struck by how much of the visit happened while we were standing still. We spent time together. Susan found ways to share James’s interest in nature. They explored a tree, paused on the path, and laughed. I have pictures of the two of them that I’m very glad we took. That is what I love about this visit. Susan came to spend time with James, and she found him right there: beside a tree, with something interesting in his hand. We didn’t go far that day. In many ways, we did. From the family album. Historical information checked against the National Park Service on October 20, 2026. Share this story A little walk to pass along. title: Communication is an ecosystem, not a device.
summary: A practical, evidence-informed field guide to multimodal communication: speech, gestures, signs, gaze, objects, photos, AAC, typing, scanning, low-tech backups, communication partners, and using what is already around you.
search: Original decorative illustration.The Communication Field Guide · Updated October 2026Communication is an ecosystem, not a device.Keep enough reliable routes open for a person to say what they mean.New England still-life illustration.For the day you haveKeep enough reliable routes open.A word. A look toward the door. A familiar gesture. The actual cereal box. A photograph on a phone. A symbol. A typed sentence. A speech-generating device. A switch. A sound. More than one of these, in the same hour. Multimodal communication means keeping enough reliable routes open that a person can say what they mean in the place, body, energy level, and moment they are actually in.Looking for the practical details?Start with what mattersThere is no prize for using only one route.01 / The whole toolboxNew England still-life illustration.A useful starting point +Use the person’s established communication.Read the full details New England still-life illustration.Room for the personUse what is already around you.02 / The useful art of improvisingKeep refusal and disagreement available.The details left inThe useful part, in full.Open just what you need.There is no prize for using only one route.+ 01 / The whole toolbox Augmentative and alternative communication is broader than a particular app or device. ASHA describes AAC as multimodal: people may combine speech or vocalizations, gestures, signs, facial expression, body movement, objects, photographs, visual supports, writing, text, symbols, communication boards or books, speech-generating technology, and different access methods. The mix can change with context, audience, purpose, motor access, fatigue, and sensory conditions. A good system therefore asks two questions at once: What does this person have to say? and what is the easiest reliable route for saying it right now? AaSpeech + vocalizationWords, approximations, sounds, laughter, intonation, and other intentional vocal signals. ✋Gesture + signPointing, reaching, conventional gestures, manual signs, and familiar movements. ◉Gaze + bodyEye gaze, facial expression, orientation, movement, and established body signals that can be confirmed. ●Real objectsThe actual cup, shoe, snack, ticket, towel, or item in front of you can make a choice concrete immediately. ▧Photos + visual scenesCamera-roll pictures, venue photos, screenshots, visual schedules, maps, and pictures of real choices. ✎Drawing + writingSketching, handwriting, note apps, typing, texting, saved phrases, and text-to-speech. ▦Symbols + low-tech AACSymbol displays, communication books, printed backups, and small situation-specific boards alongside robust language. ▣Speech-generating technologyDedicated devices, tablets, and phones with robust symbol- or text-based communication systems. ↳Switch + scanning accessDirect or indirect access that lets a communicator select from available choices using an established signal. The field ruleDo not make speech the tollbooth.Speech is one route. It should not be the price of admission to choice, attention, participation, humor, refusal, privacy, or an ordinary conversation. More than requesting A full communication life includes asking, refusing, commenting, complaining, joking, greeting, telling news, correcting someone, asking questions, changing the subject, seeking help, saying “not that,” and ending the conversation. A system that can only produce “I want” is carrying far too little of the person’s life. Behavior can tell you that something changed. It cannot safely tell you the whole sentence. Pacing, movement, vocalization, withdrawal, reaching, or a facial change may tell a familiar person that something is different. Treat that as information worth responding to, not as permission to assign a precise meaning. “Something seems different—can we figure it out?” plus an accessible way to answer protects agency better than deciding what the person meant. Use what is already around you.+ 02 / The useful art of improvising Communication does not stop because the perfect material is in another room. Real objects, signs, menus, packaging, maps, tickets, photos, screenshots, timers, calendars, a notes app, a dry-erase board, and the environment itself can all make a message easier to understand or express. These are additions and backups—not reasons to take away a person’s established AAC. At a caféUse the actual menu.Point to categories. Show the picture of the soup. Compare two real items. Let a person point, type, use their device, gesture, or say “none of these.” Keep food choice, size, drink, and “finished” as separate decisions. At the grocery storeThe shelf is already a visual display.Hold up two packages. Point to the cart. Use a saved photo of the familiar brand. Photograph a new item so it can be talked about later. The real object often carries more information than an abstract placeholder. On an outingPhotograph the next step.Take a picture of the entrance, the ticket booth, the pool door, the car, or the bench where a break can happen. A phone camera can turn an unfamiliar sequence into a concrete one in under a minute. At homeLet the house do some of the talking.Use the actual cereal box, bath towel, shoes, calendar, timer, laundry basket, or remote. Pair words and AAC with objects already attached to the routine. In a medical officeMake the invisible visible.A body diagram, mirror, photo, typed note, or showing the relevant body area can reduce language load. Prepare words such as stop, break, hurts, not sure, explain again, and where. Online or in a groupUse the side doors.Chat, advance questions, a shared document, typed responses, and a follow-up message can make participation possible when real-time turn-taking is too fast. A communication tool already in the room still counts. The aim is not to create a Pinterest-perfect support system. The aim is to make meaning easier to send and receive without taking control away from the communicator. The camera roll is a surprisingly good communication drawer. Photos can set a topic, show a person or place, represent a choice, clarify which item someone means, prepare for a visit, or help recall what happened. Use current, meaningful pictures where possible. A photograph of the actual pool is often more useful than a generic blue square labeled “swim.” Visual supports can explain what language alone leaves fuzzy. A short sequence can show where we are going, what happens first, what happens next, where a break can happen, and how we get home. Keep the sequence flexible enough for real life. If something changes, show the change rather than pretending the original plan is still true. The communication partner is part of the system.+ 03 / The person across the table matters too Research on AAC partner instruction repeatedly points to partner behavior as consequential. The device can be charged, the vocabulary can be excellent, and communication can still collapse if the people nearby rush, quiz, answer for the communicator, or only notice conventional speech. Speak to the person.Ask the communicator the question. A supporter can help with access or context without becoming the person being addressed. Wait longer than feels natural.Looking, motor planning, navigating vocabulary, composing, or switching routes takes time. Silence is not an emergency. Model, do not quiz.Use the communication system while you talk when appropriate. Demonstrate language without turning every interaction into a test. Make “no” work.Offer choices that can genuinely be refused. Include stop, break, finished, not sure, and something else. Respond to credible attempts.A word, look, gesture, device selection, typed message, or established signal deserves a response even when the answer to the request is no. Repair honestly.“I think I missed that. Can we try another way?” is better than pretending to understand. Do not move communication out of reach.Ask before touching or relocating a personal communication device. Communication access should not be treated as a reward. Check the environment.Noise, glare, seating, positioning, battery, volume, Wi-Fi, visual clutter, and fatigue can all make a familiar route much harder. Field note no. 02Partner skill can lower the effort of being understood.Good support does not make the message for the person. It makes room, time, access, and another route when the first one is difficult. Choose a primary route and a backup before you need the backup.+ 04 / Redundancy is civilized Electronics lose power. Sunlight makes screens hard to see. Pools are wet. Restaurants are loud. Motor access can change with fatigue. A familiar staff member is absent. Planning two workable routes ahead of time keeps an ordinary problem from becoming a communication emergency. YESNOSTOPBREAKHELPFINISHEDNOT SURESOMETHING ELSE Before leaving the house The person’s primary communication tools are charged, mounted, packed, or otherwise available. A low-tech or lower-effort backup covers the urgent messages that matter in this setting. At least one adult knows the person’s reliable yes/no or selection signals. Situation-specific words have been added without taking away access to the rest of the person’s language. There is a plan for water, glare, noise, a dead battery, a broken mount, or a device that suddenly refuses to cooperate. The person can refuse, change course, and end the activity—not only request it. Turn this into a field card ASHA guidance supports ongoing access to AAC and multiple modalities; concerns about ordinary recreational “screen time” do not apply to a screen being used for communication. Build the route around the setting.+ 05 / Ordinary places, different demands PoolKeep the device dry. Keep communication wet-proof.A waterproof or laminated backup can cover stop, more, out, bathroom, cold, help, finished, and something else. Establish how yes/no will work in the water. Keep the full system nearby in a safe dry place. RestaurantA menu is both language and clutter.Use the actual menu, photos, pointing, text, or a short display. Separate the decisions: entrée, side, cup or glass, more, finished. Keep “none of these” available. School or programConsistency is not sameness.Keep core language and access available across rooms and people. A brief communication profile, charging plan, backup, and access notes make the system less dependent on one familiar adult. Medical visitThe historian should not replace the patient.Ask the person first when possible. A supporter can clarify history and access while still leaving room for the patient’s own yes/no, stop, pain, fear, not sure, and questions. High stressLower effort, not expectations of personhood.Stress may make a usual communication route harder. Offer a familiar lower-effort route, reduce competing sensory demands, wait, and keep urgent messages easy to reach. New peoplePut the interaction rules on one small card.“Please speak directly to me. I communicate using [routes]. Give me about [time] to answer. If that route is hard, try [backup]. Please do not [ ].” Let AI format the support. Do not let it invent the person.+ 06 / AI can do the clerical work AI can be genuinely useful for turning known facts into a clean card, simplifying a venue’s information, organizing a visual sequence, formatting current choices, creating a plain-language version, or drafting a handoff. The safe dividing line is authorship: the tool may help organize and present information; it should not claim to know what the person thinks, wants, understands, or feels. Good useTurn real facts into a visual plan.Give the AI the actual location, sequence, photos or descriptions, break option, and way home. Ask for a short plan using only those facts. Good useMake current choices easier to scan.Paste today’s actual menu or activity choices. Ask the AI to group them clearly without adding unavailable options. Good useProduce two reading levels.Keep the meaning the same while asking for a compact card and a fuller staff note. The details stay consistent; the presentation changes. Good useTranslate a known message.Translation can help bridge languages. Preserve the original alongside the translation when precision matters and verify important wording. Do notAsk AI to read someone’s mind.Do not turn a photo, behavior, movement, or supporter’s hunch into a claimed statement of what the person wants or feels. Do notUpload private history because the prompt has an empty box.Use the minimum information needed for the communication task. A restaurant host does not need a medical chart to wait fifteen seconds for an answer. Free shared toolThe Communication Note MakerEnter the routes, yes/no signals, wait time, backup, and practical notes. It creates a printable field card, a one-page profile, and a reusable AI prompt.Open the generator → Communication belongs to the person.+ 07 / Agency first Support can make access easier without taking over the message. The aim is not for a partner to become a better guesser. The aim is for the communicator to have reliable ways to initiate, choose, refuse, clarify, disagree, repair, and end an interaction. Final selections stay with the communicator.Suggestions, prediction, modeling, or visual organization can reduce effort. The person still chooses the message. Interpretation is labeled as interpretation.If a supporter thinks a behavior may mean discomfort, say “I wonder if…” and seek confirmation rather than presenting the guess as the person’s statement. Unexpected answers are allowed.A communication system should make it possible to disagree with the supporter, pick the option nobody predicted, or introduce a new topic. Repair is shared work.When meaning is unclear, both people can slow down, change route, add context, and try again. Field note no. 03Presume a right to communicate, not a message you have already decided.Respect means access, time, useful language, and the freedom to surprise the person who thought they knew the answer. title: A welcome before you walk through the door.
summary: A toy-shop sign in Bath, England, offers something wonderfully practical: quieter music, softer lights and room to be yourself. A note on making welcome specific.
search: My Small World · Bath, EnglandA welcome before you walk through the door.A little toy-shop sign, a place built around play, and a useful idea to bring home to our own Main Streets.An AUsome Life · October 8, 2026An imagined toy-shop welcome, inspired by the story. Original editorial illustration. A photograph of a sign outside My Small World, a toy shop in Bath, England, caught my eye. It announces that the shop is autism friendly. Then it gets to the part I especially like: what that means when you actually arrive. The sign offers to lower the music, soften the lighting and give people space. It reassures visitors about excited play, noise and moments of overwhelm. It invites families to say what would help. “Give you space to be you.”From My Small World’s welcome sign That is a lovely thing to encounter before you have even opened the door. The shop behind the signA whole little world of play. My Small World is an independent toy shop in Bath’s SouthGate shopping area. In the shop’s own account of its beginnings, the idea grew from a search for a special first-birthday present in 2003. That very personal starting point feels fitting for a business whose welcome has travelled so far beyond its front door. The team describes a shop with trees, changing seasonal foliage, birdsong and shelves of books, games, toys and things to make. Play is encouraged. The pleasure of looking, touching and discovering something is part of the visit they want to offer. There is a more recent chapter, too. Revo named My Small World its 2025 Independent Operator of the Year. The award’s description highlights the newer SouthGate store, its playful interior and a sensory space for neurodivergent families. That recognition helps put the much-shared sign in context: the welcome is part of a wider approach to the shop. The relief is in the details. When an ordinary errand takes planning, a specific welcome gives you something to work with. You can picture asking for the music to come down. You know that needing a little room is something the staff have already considered. One less conversation has to begin with an explanation. On its own website, My Small World explains that its team includes autistic people and parents of autistic children. The shop describes a commitment to helping families feel comfortable, grounded in that lived experience. What stays with me is the invitation to arrive as you are. There is room in that idea for a wonderful browse, a very brief visit, a pause, or deciding to try another day. Why it stays with usRoom for the day you are having. A toy shop can hold so much promise: something to turn over in your hands, a favorite subject on a bookshelf, the pleasure of choosing. For a family like ours, that invitation also needs room for an older child, an iPad used for communication and a visit that might be shorter than expected. The particular kindness of the sign is that the adjustments are offered before anyone has to ask. It makes room for a conversation about what would help today. A person can enjoy a lively display and still want the music lowered; someone else may prefer a quiet corner or a little more time. Familiar things within reach. Original editorial illustration. Bring that welcome to our own Main Streets. A bookshop, café, farm stand or hotel can make its welcome useful in the same way: tell people what help is actually available, and make it easy to ask. A few places to begin: Be specific about sound and light. Say whether music can be lowered, which areas are quieter, and what lighting can be adjusted. Offer time and space. Explain where someone can pause and whether they can step outside and return. Ask what helps before stepping in. Welcome different ways of communicating. Give people time to point, type, use picture cards or speak through an AAC device. Address the person directly and respect their answer. Keep the welcome age respectful. Autistic teenagers and adults belong in the picture, too. Offer help without assuming someone’s interests, abilities or preferred language. Those are ideas for other businesses to consider, beyond the adjustments described on this particular sign. The best version is a promise the staff understand and can keep.It can be as ordinary as telling a visitor, “We can lower the music. Would that help?” Then listening to the answer. A welcome has room for “yes,” “no,” “later,” and an answer given without speech. A small sign can start a conversation. For our family, the practical details belong right alongside the lovely ones. The invitation to look around matters. So does knowing that asking for a change will be met with understanding. I would love to see more of that on our own Main Streets: a clear, ordinary welcome, with enough detail to make walking through the door feel a little easier. If Bath is on your listStart with SouthGate’s current shop listing and My Small World’s contact page. The listings give different street numbers following the shop’s move, so confirm the entrance before setting out. The shop’s published telephone number is +44 (0)1225 312943.Ask what can be adjusted during your visit, how the sensory space works and whether there is a quieter time to come. Check the route into the shop, space to move around and nearby accessible toilets separately. A welcoming sign is helpful; each family will still have its own practical questions. About this noteThis is a reflection on a sign spotted online and the shop’s published approach, rather than a report from a family visit. The sign has circulated for years; we are sharing the idea, not announcing a new policy.Read My Small World’s story and autism-friendly approach or contact the shop before a visit.
